svg.title: How could you actually filter out a microplastic?
svg.desc: Mind-map of eighteen filtration mechanisms grouped into four families — barrier and membrane filtration, field-driven separation including resonant sound and magnetics, chemical and bio aggregation, and push/pressure mechanisms — each broken into subsections, tagged by portability and by whether its own material could shed microplastic back into the water.
svg.text: How could you actually filter out a microplastic?
Eighteen filtration mechanisms across four families — how you physically block a particle, how a field or flow pulls it out with
no media to clog, how you chemically make it big enough to catch, and what actually pushes the water through any of the above.
Every card also marks whether its own material could shed microplastic back into the water it just cleaned.
size exclusion — a physical wall the particle can’t pass
Pores over 0.1 µm in a PVDF or polyethersulfone sheet strain
out larger fragments and fibres by size alone — the coarsest,
2–100 nm pores reject 90–99% of microplastics including fine
fibres — the workhorse stage in most household MP filter
fouls faster than MF, needs backwash
Sub-2 nm pores catch nanoplastics and dissolved contaminants
together, but need pump pressures of several bar — hard to run
without mains power in a handheld device.
highest energy cost of any barrier option
A sintered alumina or diatomite ‘candle’ strains water by pore
size alone, under gravity; scrubbable and reusable for years,
with nothing plastic in the flow path to shed.
classic gravity-fed form factor, low cost/unit
Finer ceramic pores (2–100 nm) push rejection to 95–99% while
keeping the same non-shedding, scrub-clean advantage — the
A washable woven steel screen (down to roughly 40–100 µm)
strips out fibres and large fragments before the fine stage;
fully metal, so it cannot itself shed microplastic.
prefilter role, extends downstream filter life
Water percolates through graded silica sand and gravel;
particles get trapped in the pore network by depth, not a
single sieving plane — the oldest water-treatment trick there
bulky for a handheld unit, needs backwash
no filter media to clog — a force pulls the particle out
Iron-oxide nanoparticles dosed into the water adsorb onto
then a permanent magnet pulls the whole composite out in
Ultrasound pulsed through a resonating steel tube sets up a
standing wave; its acoustic radiation force pushes particles
to pressure nodes for collection — like a magnet sorting iron
A shaped acoustic chamber sweeps fibres toward an outlet using
inaudible high-frequency ultrasound — purely physical, no
chemicals, and scales from a 20 L/hr bench unit to a 5–10 t/hr
Fibres are permanently or self-charged by friction with the
passing water, so they attract polarised microplastic
particles electrostatically on top of ordinary size sieving —
most electret media are themselves charged PP fibre
Tangential inflow spins water into a vortex; denser or larger
particles fling to the wall and exit the underflow while
cleaner water exits the core — no membrane to clog or replace,
mini-hydrocyclone variants tested at bench scale
Fine bubbles injected into the water attach to hydrophobic
microplastic surfaces and float them to a skimmable top layer;
often paired with a mini-hydrocyclone for a bigger efficiency
make the particle bigger — then it’s easy to catch
A metal-salt coagulant neutralises the microplastic’s surface
charge so particles clump into flocs large enough to settle or
strain out — the standard municipal-plant trick, adapted down.
leaves a metal-ion residue — needs post-rinse
A biopolymer extracted from crustacean shells binds
microplastics by charge neutralisation just like alum, but is
itself biodegradable — no synthetic residue left behind in the
An electric current dissolves a sacrificial metal electrode in
situ, generating the coagulant ions on demand — no chemical
bottle to carry, but it consumes the electrode and needs a
metal-ion residue; electrode is a consumable
A living or dried fungal hyphae network physically traps
microplastics in its mesh while also bio-adsorbing them onto
its cell walls — the whole filter medium is compostable when
An oyster-inspired sponge of nanocellulose and chitosan fibres
offers huge surface area for microplastics to adsorb onto; the
whole sponge is lifted out and replaced — biodegradable, no
how the water actually moves through whichever stage above
An elevated chamber lets gravity alone drive water down
through the filter stage below — zero power, zero moving
parts, but slow, and needs enough height to build usable
pairs classically with a sand bed or ceramic candle
The user’s own hand pressure pushes water through on demand —
the LifeStraw/Sawyer approach — fast flow, no battery, but
use food-grade silicone bulb, not PVC
Rollers compress a flexible tube in sequence, pushing water
along without the pump mechanism ever touching the water
itself — self-priming, contamination-safe, cheap small motors.
use silicone tubing, not PVC — wear is the risk
A reciprocating diaphragm or piston generates the higher
pressure (several bar) that UF/NF-grade membranes actually
need — more flow and pressure than a peristaltic pump, more
Suction pulls water through the filter from the downstream
side instead of pushing from upstream — a simple mechanical
action, easy to prototype with off-the-shelf syringes.
glass or inert-plastic barrel, low wear
Mechanical energy stored ahead of time (a compressed spring, a
pressurised gas cartridge) releases on demand for a burst of
flow — no continuous user effort, but needs re-charging or a
seals/gaskets wear over the cartridge’s life
Caution — no plastic shed, but watch a wear part or residue
May shed — the medium is itself a plastic
HOW TO PROCEED — WHAT TO PROTOTYPE, WHAT TO AVOID
Eighteen mechanisms across four families, and only three of them are size-exclusion membranes — the rest use fields, chemistry or
flow instead of a medium that can clog. The standout combination for a handheld MPx unit: a ceramic candle prefilter feeding a
chitosan or nanocellulose polishing sponge, pushed by a peristaltic pump with food-grade silicone tubing — nothing in that flow path
is itself plastic, so the filter can't reintroduce what it just removed. Acoustic and magnetic separation are worth watching next:
no consumable media to replace at all, but today's bench hardware (steel resonating tubes, dosed nanoparticles) is still too bulky
and power-hungry to shrink into a handheld device yet. Avoid raw PVDF/PES/PTFE membrane fibres, PP electret nonwovens, and PVC
tubing or gaskets — all shed microplastic themselves under wear.
Sources: OAE Publish Environ. Chem. Eng. Health 2026 (ceramic membranes); PMC 2025 (pressure-driven membrane review); ACS Axial / New Mexico Tech
(ultrasonic acoustic focusing); H&M Foundation — Acousweep (sweeping-chamber acoustic separation); Wiley Small 2024 & PMC 2022 (magnetic Fe3O4 separation);
RSC Sustainability 2026 (biopolymer/nanocellulose filtration); ACS Appl. Polym. Mater. 2021 (chitosan sponge); ScienceDirect 2021–25 (coagulation,
electrocoagulation, hydrocyclone + microbubble flotation). Filter/push mechanisms are a new axis alongside MPx_Detection_Methods_Comparison.docx and
